newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Further deterioration seen.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Further deterioration seen.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices are expected to continue falling Tuesday, amid poor sentiment and the desire by inevstors to cheapen up securities ahead of note auctions later this week.

"I don't dislike the market, but the momentum, isn't good" said Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities International Inc. "Retail is real leery .. people are nervous about protecting capital."
Verterano predicts Treasury yields moving up another four to five basis points across the curve in the next two days.
"People are trying to get the market as cheap as they can," he said.
Treasuries moved lower Monday, as the dollar slumped, oil prices rose, and as industrial production was reported higher than expected in November.
Tuesday features a light day as far as fundamentals go, with October housing starts due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, and the Federal Reserve's policy-setting meeting in the morning.
Market participants said that the Fed meeting is unlikely to produce a reaction, barring the improbable scenario that the Fed shocks the market by altering interest rates.
As for housing starts, a Reuters poll found economists on average expect starts to have risen to a 1.39 million annual unit rate in October from a 1.366 million rate in September.
"It is not going to be a dull day," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Platt, though, forsees the minutes from the November Fed meeting -- to be released Friday aftermnoon - as the key piece of information of the week.

In the near term, players said the market would focus on stock prices. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 50 points early Monday, then fell 100 points off its highs, to close down 37 points. If stocks continue to struggle, players said, it could help bonds.
Meanwhile, the market is seen watching oil prices, which rose Monday, and the dollar, which fell.
These factors could determine the success of this week's auctions. The Treasury on Wednesday will sell $18.25 billion two-year notes, followed by $12.5 billion five-year notes on Thursday.

Traders said that with the market so cautious, dealers will likely push up the yields on both issues. The when-issued two-year note was at 5.81 percent late Monday, while the when-issued five-year note was at 6.14 percent.

The two-year note was down 3/32 at 99-21/32 to yield 5.81 percent. The 10-year note was at 100-28/32, down 14/32, to yield 6.37 percent, and the 30-year bond was off 22/32 at 98-10/32 to yield 6.63 percent.
